title: StableID: An Iterative Graph-Based Framework for Persistent Entity Identification in Evolving Industrial Data Systems
research_question: How can graph-based entity-resolution systems preserve stable, auditable identifiers for real-world entities as identifying evidence and connected components evolve over repeated executions?
methodology: The paper develops StableID, an iterative graph framework that feeds prior grouping results into subsequent executions, applies deterministic identifier dominance when components merge, and generates time-scoped identifiers for newly observed entities. Entity groups are represented as connected components, so identifying edges induce transitive component membership. The framework is evaluated over ten iterative executions on large-scale entity data modeled on multi-state voter-registration structure; the data-availability statement characterizes the specific entity-level datasets generated for the study as synthetic. The evaluation compares identifier retention and convergence against independently recomputed connected-component identifiers and reports operational behavior at more than 200 million records.

key_findings.finding: Feeding prior entity-group assignments into later graph executions and retaining a dominant historical identifier substantially reduces identifier churn across repeated runs.

StableID maintains roughly 95% or better identifier retention through most iterative runs, while the naive independently recomputed connected-component baseline exhibits about 40% identifier churn on otherwise stable data.

The graph converges as new identifying evidence is absorbed: reported merge counts fall from 12,847 in iteration 8 to 847 in iteration 9 and 12 in iteration 10 while the total identifier count stabilizes near 7.63 million.
key_findings.section: Results / Component Convergence and Merge Saturation

key_findings.finding: The deterministic dominance rule preserves the identifier carrying the greatest historical support when previously separate components merge, making identifier evolution auditable rather than arbitrary.
The evaluation does not establish precision or recall against definitive real-world identity ground truth because such ground truth was unavailable for the protected voter-identity setting.

The framework does not provide evidence for partial, overlapping, or non-transitive continuity relationships: connected-component membership instead represents a transitive equivalence relation once identifying edges connect records.
The study does not evaluate enterprise email, chat, conversational threads, or organizational work-item linking.

limitations: Definitive person-level identity ground truth was unavailable, so the evaluation cannot directly measure entity-resolution precision and recall against verified identities.
The specific entity-level evaluation datasets are synthetic even though their structure is based on voter-registration and election-domain data.
Connected components force transitive equivalence and cannot natively represent partial, overlapping, directional, subevent, or non-transitive continuity relations.
The empirical study concerns industrial entity identification rather than enterprise email, chat, or longitudinal work-item continuity.
The evaluated execution model is oriented toward repeated batch-style runs rather than continuously updated conversational workflows.
Suggested applicability to customer, supply-chain, medical, and IoT identity systems is broader than the domains directly evaluated.
raw_claims: StableID treats identifiers as persistent operational assets rather than recomputing arbitrary component labels at every run.
Prior grouping information is fed back into the graph so historical identity can influence subsequent executions.
When components merge, a deterministic dominance rule selects which historical identifier survives.
New entities receive identifiers scoped to the execution in which they are first created, reducing collision risk.
Identifier retention remains high across repeated executions even when identifying relationships are added or removed.
The number of component merges declines sharply in the final iterations as the graph approaches a stable state.
The implementation was exercised at a scale exceeding 200 million records.
The evaluation reports identifier stability, component convergence, and merge saturation rather than supervised identity accuracy.
Definitive person-level ground truth was not available for validating whether every graph component corresponds to one true individual.
A connected-component model makes identity membership transitive and does not encode graded or overlapping continuity.
